title: How Much Faster Does AI Actually Make Programmers?
question: How much faster does AI actually make programmers?
alternates: 2x, 10x, or Slower? What the Trials Found
The METR Study Everyone Cites, Explained
premise: Field trials put the average gain in the twenties: Microsoft/Accenture (4,867 developers, 26% more weekly PRs), Google (96 engineers, about 21% less time on an enterprise task, confidence interval crossing zero) and Shan's field study (18% more user stories, self-selected usage). METR 2025 found the opposite sign for 16 experienced open-source maintainers in their own mature repos: 19% slower with early-2025 tools. The 10x claim has no supporting measurement; the field gain and Anthropic's self-reported 50% bound it, and neither measured agentic coding. METR's 2026 update says the slowdown was probably specific to early 2025 but calls its new data very weak evidence because of selection effects. Google's migration figures (50% to 89% savings) are bespoke pipelines and engineers' estimates, context only.
whyWatch: The claims run from 10x to 'it slows you down', and both extremes cite studies. The trials fit together once you look at who was measured doing what.
tension: Ten-times claims against field trials in the twenties of percent and one trial that found experienced maintainers 19% slower.

arc.hook: Three numbers on screen: 10x, 26%, minus 19%. All of them come with a study attached.
arc.conflict: The hype and the slowdown both cite trials; the question is what each trial measured.
arc.evidence: Microsoft/Accenture, Google and Shan on real work; METR 2025 on mature repos with experts; METR 2026 on what changed and why it cannot tell; the absence of any 10x measurement.
arc.resolution: Twenties of percent on average work, less or negative for experts in familiar code, unknown for today's agentic tools; 10x is unmeasured.
arc.takeaway: Expect a quarter, not a multiple, and expect less on the code you know best.

questions.question: How much faster does AI actually make programmers?

central.text: AI tools slowed experienced open-source developers working on their own familiar codebases (METR 2025 RCT)

questions.premise: Field trials put the average gain in the twenties: Microsoft/Accenture (4,867 developers, 26% more weekly PRs), Google (96 engineers, about 21% less time on an enterprise task, confidence interval crossing zero) and Shan's field study (18% more user stories, self-selected usage). METR 2025 found the opposite sign for 16 experienced open-source maintainers in their own mature repos: 19% slower with early-2025 tools. The 10x claim has no supporting measurement; the field gain and Anthropic's self-reported 50% bound it, and neither measured agentic coding. METR's 2026 update says the slowdown was probably specific to early 2025 but calls its new data very weak evidence because of selection effects. Google's migration figures (50% to 89% savings) are bespoke pipelines and engineers' estimates, context only.
questions.tension: Ten-times claims against field trials in the twenties of percent and one trial that found experienced maintainers 19% slower.
questions.whyWatch: The claims run from 10x to 'it slows you down', and both extremes cite studies. The trials fit together once you look at who was measured doing what.

arc.hook: Three numbers on screen: 10x, 26%, minus 19%. All of them come with a study attached.
arc.conflict: The hype and the slowdown both cite trials; the question is what each trial measured.
arc.evidence: Microsoft/Accenture, Google and Shan on real work; METR 2025 on mature repos with experts; METR 2026 on what changed and why it cannot tell; the absence of any 10x measurement.
arc.resolution: Twenties of percent on average work, less or negative for experts in familiar code, unknown for today's agentic tools; 10x is unmeasured.
arc.takeaway: Expect a quarter, not a multiple, and expect less on the code you know best.

questions.question: Do developers know whether AI is actually making them faster?

central.text: Studies disagree on whether developers overestimate how much AI tools speed them up

questions.premise: The disagreement is the story and it is well measured on both sides. METR 2025 (16 experienced open-source developers, 246 tasks in their own mature repos, early-2025 tools) found a 19% slowdown against a forecast of 24% faster and an after-the-fact estimate of 20% faster; experts predicted 38-39%. Peng's 2023 Copilot trial (freelancers, a greenfield HTTP server task) found a 55.8% speedup that participants underestimated at about 35%. METR's 2026 update adds that self-reports can be very unreliable and that its new data are too selection-biased to measure. The likely explanation, task familiarity and codebase maturity, is the resolution the video should offer as a hypothesis, not a finding.
questions.tension: METR: developers forecast 24% faster, felt 20% faster, were 19% slower. Peng's Copilot trial: both groups guessed about 35% and the measured gain was 55.8%. Overestimate in one, underestimate in the other.
questions.whyWatch: Every developer has a feeling about this. Two randomized trials checked the feeling against the stopwatch and got opposite answers, which is the most useful thing a viewer can learn about their own estimate.

arc.hook: Ask the viewer to guess how much faster AI makes them, then show what happened when two trials asked the same of their participants.
arc.conflict: Two randomized trials, opposite errors: experienced maintainers overestimated and got slower; freelancers on a fresh task underestimated and got much faster.
arc.evidence: METR's forecast-versus-measured numbers and acceptance rates; Peng's estimate-versus-measured numbers; METR 2026's warning about self-reports and selection.
arc.resolution: Perception tracks effort saved on the parts AI does, not time spent on the parts it creates; which dominates depends on task familiarity and codebase maturity (a hypothesis both papers gesture at).
arc.takeaway: Measure, don't ask: time a week of comparable tasks with and without the tool.
